title: Where knowledge begins
sum: Chapter 1 opens the book with a title, a purpose and a motto. The proverbs are for "knowing wisdom and discipline" (1:2): for the naive, for the young and even for the wise (1:4–5). Then comes the line that governs everything after it: "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (1:7).

Two voices follow. A father warns his son against a gang that invites him to ambush the innocent and share the loot; their trap will catch themselves (1:8–19). Then Wisdom appears as a woman shouting in the streets, warning the naive, the mockers and the fools that if they ignore her now, she will not answer when disaster comes (1:20–33).
readings: Read as a school book

The prologue (1:2–6) reads like the opening of an Egyptian instruction: it names its readers and its aims. The father's talk and Wisdom's speech teach the first lessons of any education: choose your company, and listen while there is time. On this reading the chapter is practical, addressed to a real young man who could be drawn into violence.
Read as a theological gate

Others read 1:7 as the key to the whole book: wisdom is not only skill but begins in reverence for the LORD. Wisdom's speech, with its prophetic warnings and its promise to 'pour out my spirit' (1:23), shows that she speaks for God. On this reading the chapter introduces Wisdom as a figure who will grow in chapters 8–9 into the LORD's companion at creation.

views.H: The setting is a household or a school in Jerusalem where a young man of good family is being prepared for adult life. Gangs of robbers who waylaid travelers were a real danger (Hosea 6:9; Judges 9:25), and a young man without land might be tempted to join one. Wisdom's speech takes place where a city's life happened: the street, the squares and the gates (1:20–21).
views.C: Most scholars read 1:1–7 as the editor's preface to the finished book, written when chapters 1–9 were added to older collections, probably in the Persian period. The prologue's list of wisdom words (1:2–6) introduces the vocabulary of the whole book. Wisdom's speech (1:20–33) borrows the forms of prophetic judgment speeches, especially Jeremiah 7 and Isaiah 65–66, which suggests a writer who knew the prophets.
views.W: Egyptian instructions begin as Proverbs does, with a heading naming the teacher and a statement of purpose. The Instruction of Amenemope opens: 'The beginning of the teaching for life, the instructions for well-being', and lists the skills it will teach. The father's warnings against bad company have parallels in Any and Ahiqar. Wisdom's speech has no close Egyptian parallel; a goddess threatening those who ignore her is rare.
views.J: Rabbinic readers took the 'father' as God and the 'mother' as the community of Israel, or the father as the written Torah and the mother as the oral Torah (Rashi on 1:8). The gang of 1:10–19 was read as the wicked who lure Israel to idolatry. Wisdom's call in the streets is the Torah's voice, heard daily in the houses of study.
views.X: 1 Clement 57, about AD 96, quotes Wisdom's warning in 1:23–33 at length, as Scripture. Paul quotes the line shared with Isaiah 59:7 about feet that rush to shed blood (Romans 3:15). Christian readers have seen in Wisdom's promise to 'pour out my spirit' (1:23) a foretaste of Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and in her rejected call a picture of Christ's lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37).

deep.b: For chapters 1–9 the Hebrew text is the Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), checked through the site's own Hebrew text and its machine list of the codex's Ketiv and Qere readings. The Greek is cited from Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus (B), with its notes on Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), and compared with Rahlfs' critical text. 'The Greek' means the Old Greek as printed by Rahlfs; a reading found only in one codex is named by that codex. The readings of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, of the Syriac Peshitta, of the Targum and of Jerome's Latin are given as reported by Toy's commentary and by Fox's edition. The Qumran fragments 4QProv-a, which preserves parts of 1:27–2:1, and 4QProv-b, which preserves parts of 7:9 and 7:11 among others, are cited as reported in their official edition (DJD 16); as reported there, they differ from the Masoretic Text in these chapters only in spelling and small details, not in sense.

The book's motto (1:7) returns at the end of the introduction (9:10) and at the end of the book (31:30), framing the whole. The 'fear of the LORD' is not panic but the reverence that knows who God is and lives accordingly; the book defines it as hating evil (8:13) and links it with humility (15:33; 22:4) and long life (10:27; 14:27). It is both the first step and the foundation: one does not outgrow it. Job 28:28 and Psalm 111:10 make the same claim, which suggests it was a common saying among Israel's teachers.

The word reshit in 1:7 may mean 'beginning' (the first step), 'best part' (the chief thing) or 'foundation' (see the note at 1:7). The parallel line in 9:10 uses techillah, which means 'start'. Many teachers have read the motto as Augustine and Anselm did faith: one does not first gain knowledge and then decide to fear God; reverence comes first and opens the way to understanding.

Wisdom speaks like a prophet. Her 'How long?' (1:22) echoes Jeremiah, and her 'Since I called and you said no' (1:24) echoes Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 almost word for word. She speaks of pouring out her spirit (1:23), as God does in Joel 2:28. Yet she does not say 'Thus says the LORD'. She speaks in her own name, and those who refuse her are said to refuse 'the fear of the LORD' (1:29). This is the first hint of what chapter 8 will make explicit: Wisdom speaks for God because she comes from God.

Her laughter at the disaster of fools (1:26) has troubled readers. Most commentators take it as the bitter irony of a teacher whose warnings were ignored: the consequences arrive, and there is nothing left to say. The speech is not cruel to those still listening, for it ends with a promise: "the one who listens to me will settle in safety" (1:33).

echoes: Isaiah 59:7; Romans 3:15; Isaiah 65:12; Isaiah 66:4; Jeremiah 7:13; Psalm 111:10; Job 28:28; Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17; Matthew 23:37; 1 Kings 4:29–34

settings.by: The editor who gathered the book, speaking in Solomon's name
settings.to: Every reader of the book: the naive, the young and the already wise
settings.when: at the opening of the finished collection
settings.why: To say what the book is for and how to use it: the sayings teach skill in living, but only those who begin with the fear of the LORD will understand them. Knowing that the preface was written for the whole book means the motto of 1:7 governs every saying that follows, even those that never mention God.
settings.readers: For the first readers, probably Judeans of the Persian period, the preface offered Solomon's authority and a program of education for a people without a king.
views: Traditional readers take 1:1–7 as Solomon's introduction to his own teaching.
Most scholars think it was written last, by the editors who joined the collections.

settings.what: Do not go with the gang
settings.to: His son, a young man about to leave home
settings.when: before the son faces the pressure of violent companions
settings.why: To warn him that easy money through violence ends in death for those who seek it, and to give him the words to refuse ('do not go along', 1:10). The father quotes the gang's pitch so that the son will recognize it when he hears it.
settings.readers: Later readers heard any invitation to profit by harming others, from robbers to corrupt officials.
views: A real father warns his son, as parents did in Israel's villages and towns (Westermann; Golka).
A teacher addresses a pupil as 'my son', as Egyptian scribal instructions do (Carr; Crenshaw).
The talk was kept and placed here by the editors of Persian-period Judea to form young men for life in the community (Fox; Washington).

settings.to: The naive, mockers and fools in the city's streets and gates
settings.when: in public, while there is still time to listen
settings.why: To call the careless to turn before disaster, and to say plainly that a day will come when it is too late. The speech uses the prophets' language, so the reader knows that refusing Wisdom is refusing God (1:29).
settings.readers: For the book's readers, Wisdom's warning echoed the prophets' warnings before the exile, which had come true; they were to listen this time.
views: Most read Wisdom here as a personification of the teaching of the wise.
Others see in her a heavenly being or an aspect of God, as chapter 8 develops.

title: If you search for her like silver
sum: Chapter 2 is one long 'if... then' sentence. If the son takes in his father's words and searches for wisdom as for buried treasure (2:1–4), then he will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God (2:5–8). Wisdom will enter his heart and guard him (2:9–11).

It will rescue him from two dangers: men whose talk is upside down and whose roads are crooked (2:12–15), and the strange woman, who has walked out on her husband and forgotten the covenant of her God, and whose house sinks down to death (2:16–19). The chapter ends with the promise of the land for the upright and the warning that the wicked will be pulled up out of it (2:20–22).
readings: Read as a curriculum

The chapter reads like a table of contents for chapters 3–7: seeking wisdom (3–4), the evil man (4:14–19; 6:12–19), the strange woman (5–7). It shows how the father's teaching works: effort, then gift, then protection.
Read as a choice between two women

The chapter introduces the pattern that rules chapters 1–9: the young man stands between Wisdom, who enters his heart (2:10), and the strange woman, who leads to death (2:18). Many readers see the strange woman as both a real danger and a symbol of folly, so that the choice is about a whole way of life.

views.H: The son is a young Israelite who will soon marry and manage a household. The danger of an affair with a married woman is real and legal: adultery was a capital crime (Deuteronomy 22:22), and an injured husband could ruin the man (6:34–35). Mention of 'the land' (2:21–22) assumes a society of family landholdings.
views.C: Scholars debate who the 'strange woman' was. Most see an Israelite adulteress (2:17). Some see a foreign woman and connect the warnings with the Persian-period debates over marriage to foreigners (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13). Others see a figure of folly. The Greek turns her into 'evil counsel', and the Qumran poem 4Q184 makes her a demonic temptress. The chapter's 22 verses imitate the length of an alphabet poem.
views.W: Egyptian instructions warn against the 'woman from abroad'. The Instruction of Any says: 'Beware of a woman who is a stranger, one not known in her town... a deep water whose course is unknown', and adds that she has no witnesses. The Babylonian Counsels of Wisdom advise against marrying a temple prostitute. Proverbs shares the warning but grounds it in 'the covenant of her God' (2:17).
views.J: Many Jewish readers took the strange woman as heresy or idolatry: Rashi reads her as the foreign worship that pulls Israel from the Torah, and the Talmud warns that 'all who go in to her never return' applies to heresy (Bavli Avodah Zarah 17a). The promise of the land (2:21) was read of Israel's inheritance and of the world to come.
views.X: Christian readers applied the search for wisdom to seeking Christ, 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Colossians 2:3), and the strange woman to false teaching and to the 'great prostitute' of Revelation 17. Many preachers have kept the plain sense too, using the chapter to teach faithfulness in marriage.

deep.b:
Hebrew calls her 'ishshah zarah, 'the strange woman', and nokhriyyah, 'the foreign woman'. Zar means someone outside a circle: outside one's family, one's household, the priesthood or the people. Nokhri usually means a foreigner. The two words in parallel could mean 'another man's wife' (outside your marriage) or 'a woman of another people'.

The text gives clues. She has left 'the close friend she had when she was young' and forgotten 'the covenant of her God' (2:17), so she is married and bound by a covenant, probably an Israelite. In chapter 7 her husband is away on business (7:19–20), and in chapter 6 she is 'a man's wife' (6:26). Most commentators therefore see an adulteress, called 'strange' because she belongs to someone else (Fox; Waltke).

Others note that 'foreign' is a strong word. Joseph Blenkinsopp and Harold Washington connect the warnings with Judea after the exile, when marriages with women outside the community threatened family land and identity (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Gustav Boström thought she was a devotee of a foreign love goddess (7:14). Claudia Camp sees her as a literary figure who gathers every kind of 'otherness' feared by the community and stands opposite Lady Wisdom. Many readers combine these views: a real danger, described so that she becomes a symbol of the road to death.

Chapters 2, 5, 6 and 7 are warnings given by a father to a son. They speak about women, not to them. Carol Newsom has shown how the father's speech divides women into two kinds, the wife and Wisdom on one side and the strange woman on the other, and makes the young man's choice between them the test of his loyalty to his father's world. Gale Yee and others have argued that the strange woman carries the fears of a male society about women's speech, sexuality and independence.

Other readers point out that the strange woman is condemned for deceit and adultery, sins the book condemns in men just as strongly (1:10–19; 6:12–19; 6:32), and that Proverbs also praises the teaching of mothers (1:8; 31:1), describes Wisdom herself as a woman and ends with a woman of strength who runs a household and a business (31:10–31). Both points can be held together. The warnings speak to a real danger to young men and their families, and they are written from a man's point of view in a society where men held the power.

echoes: Job 28:1–12; Matthew 13:44; Colossians 2:3; Hosea 4:1; Malachi 2:14–16; Psalm 37:9–11; Matthew 5:5; Ezra 10:2; 1 Kings 11:1–8

settings.what: What wisdom will save you from
settings.to: His son, a young man on the edge of marriage and public life
settings.when: as the son begins to choose his own companions and his own road
settings.why: To persuade the son that seeking wisdom is worth the effort, because wisdom comes from the LORD and protects against the two great dangers of youth: violent and twisted men, and the strange woman. The single long sentence makes the point that everything follows from the first 'if'.
settings.readers: Later readers in Judea heard the promise that the upright would remain in the land (2:21) as a word about who would belong to the restored community.
views: A real father prepares his son for marriage and adult life.
A teacher in the Persian period warns young men against marriages and alliances that would weaken the community (Blenkinsopp; Washington).

title: Trust the LORD with your whole heart
sum: Chapter 3 gathers three talks. The first (3:1–12) asks the son to keep his father's teaching, to trust the LORD rather than his own understanding, to honor the LORD with his first produce, and to accept the LORD's discipline as a son accepts a father's. The second (3:13–20) is a hymn: "Happy is the person who has found wisdom" (3:13), worth more than silver and gold, a tree of life, the wisdom by which the LORD founded the earth.

The third (3:21–35) promises safe sleep to those who keep wisdom and then turns to neighbors: do good when you can, do not put off paying, do not plot harm, do not envy the violent. The LORD curses the house of the wicked and blesses the home of the righteous. "Mockers he mocks, / but the humble he gives his favor" (3:34).
readings: Read as a promise of reward
3:1–10 promises long life, health and full barns to those who trust and honor the LORD. Read alone, it can sound like a guarantee of prosperity, and some have preached it that way.
Read with 3:11–12

The next verses say that the LORD also disciplines those he loves, so the son must not give up when life is hard. Read together, the chapter teaches trust that holds in both blessing and correction, which is how Hebrews 12 reads it.

views.H: The world is agricultural: barns, vats, firstfruits (3:9–10). The neighbor of 3:27–30 lives next door and may be owed wages or a loan. A wise son is expected to manage land and keep peace in a village where everyone depends on everyone.
views.C: Scholars note that 3:1–12 alternates commands and reasons in a regular pattern, while 3:13–20 is a separate hymn that anticipates chapter 8. Some think 3:19–20, on creation by wisdom, was added by the editor who wrote chapter 8.
views.W: Wisdom holding long life in one hand and riches in the other (3:16) resembles Egyptian images of Maat, the goddess of order, holding the sign of life. Kayatz argued for direct influence; others think the image was common. 'Do not say to your neighbor, "Go on, come back later"' (3:28) has parallels in Egyptian advice on paying debts promptly.
views.J: 'To those who grab hold of her she is a tree of life' (3:18) and 'Her roads are roads of delight, and every one of her paths is peace' (3:17) are sung in the synagogue when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark: Wisdom is the Torah. The command to honor the LORD from one's wealth (3:9) was linked to giving to the poor and to the Temple offerings.
views.X: Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes 3:11–12 from the Greek to encourage persecuted Christians. James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 quote 3:34 from the Greek: 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.' 3:5–6 is among the most memorized verses in Protestant devotion. Many Christian teachers apply 3:9–10 to tithing and generous giving; some preachers of the 'prosperity gospel' read it as a promise of wealth, which most Christian traditions reject.

deep.b:
The Hebrew of 3:12 says that the LORD rebukes the one he loves 'the way a father treats the son he takes pleasure in'. The Greek read the second line differently: 'and he whips every son he receives'. Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the Greek and builds a sermon on it: hardship is a sign that God treats the readers as his children; a father who never corrects his son does not treat him as a son (Hebrews 12:7–11). The verses became a classic text for Christian teaching on suffering, alongside Job 5:17, "Think how fortunate a man is when God corrects him!"

Jewish teachers drew a similar lesson. The Talmud calls such suffering 'chastisements of love' (yissurin shel ahavah), sent to the righteous for their good (Bavli Berakhot 5a). Both traditions also warn against using the verses to explain every misfortune: the book of Job shows that suffering may have no such reason the sufferer can see.

deep.h: Grace to the humble: 3:34 in James and 1 Peter
deep.b: The Hebrew of 3:34 is a wordplay: 'Mockers he mocks.' The Greek translated it 'The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble'. James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 both quote the Greek, word for word, as Scripture, which suggests the saying was well known in the early church. The Hebrew and the Greek agree on the second line, God's favor (chen, Greek charis, 'grace') to the humble, and the New Testament made that line a summary of the gospel's call to humility.

echoes: Hebrews 12:5–11; Job 5:17; Revelation 3:19; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5; Deuteronomy 6:5; Deuteronomy 8:5; Psalm 104:24; Genesis 2:9; Exodus 23:19; Malachi 3:10

settings.what: Trust the LORD and honor him
settings.to: His son
settings.when: as the son begins to manage his own household and land
settings.why: To join the father's teaching to trust in the LORD: obedience brings long life and peace (3:1–4), trust must be total (3:5–8), wealth is to honor God (3:9–10), and hardship is the discipline of a loving father, not rejection (3:11–12).
settings.readers: Later Jewish writers (compare 2 Maccabees 6:12–16) and the readers of Hebrews took suffering as a father's discipline, and Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes 3:11–12 for persecuted Christians.
views: A father teaches a son who will inherit land and a household (Westermann; Golka).
A teacher trains future officials or scribes, who learned such texts by heart (Carr; Crenshaw).
Editors in Persian-period Judea gathered the talks to form young men in covenant loyalty (Fox; Blenkinsopp).

settings.what: Happy is the one who finds wisdom
settings.to: Any listener; the son is not named
settings.when: between two of the father's talks
settings.why: To praise wisdom as the greatest treasure and to ground the father's teaching in the order of creation: the wisdom the son is asked to seek is the wisdom by which the LORD made the world (3:19).
settings.readers: The synagogue sings 3:17–18 of the Torah; Christian readers heard 3:19 with John 1:3.

settings.to: His son
settings.when: as he takes his place among neighbors and creditors
settings.why: To show that wisdom is practical: it lets a man sleep in peace and makes him generous, prompt in paying, and peaceful with his neighbors, while the LORD sides with the humble against mockers.

title: Three generations and two roads
sum: In chapter 4 the father tells his sons what his own father taught him when he was a boy: "Acquire wisdom; acquire understanding" (4:5). Wisdom is to be loved like a bride, and she will crown the one who holds her (4:6–9).

Then the father sets out two roads: the straight road of wisdom, on which a young man can run without stumbling, and the dark path of the wicked, who cannot sleep until they have done harm (4:10–19). The road of the righteous is like the dawn, growing brighter until full day (4:18). The chapter ends with a lesson on the body: guard the heart above all, keep the mouth straight, the eyes forward and the feet level (4:20–27).
readings: Read as family memory
The father's memory of his own father (4:3–4) makes the teaching a heritage: wisdom passes down the generations. Jewish readers heard Solomon recalling David.
Read as a map

The chapter's road images (4:11–19, 26–27) turn the moral life into a journey with a destination. Christian readers connected it with the 'two ways' of Jesus' teaching (Matthew 7:13–14) and the Didache.

views.H: A father teaching 'sons' in the plural may be a real father with several children or a teacher with pupils. The three-generation chain (4:3–4) fits a society where teaching was passed down in families and trades.
views.C: The chapter is made of three short instructions (4:1–9, 10–19, 20–27), each with an opening call to listen. Scholars note that 4:18–19 seem out of order (19 would follow 17 naturally), and some move them. The Greek omits 4:7 and adds two verses after 4:27.
views.W: Egyptian teachers often stress that their teaching came from their fathers: Ptahhotep asks permission to teach his son what the ancestors heard from the gods. The image of a straight path and a crooked one appears in Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts as well.
views.J: Rashi and the midrash read 4:3 as Solomon speaking of David (compare 1 Chronicles 22:5; 29:1). Rabbi Akiva proved from 4:2 that the Torah is 'a precious instrument' (Mishnah Avot 3:14). 'Guard your heart' (4:23) became a theme of Jewish ethical writing.
views.X: Hebrews 12:13 quotes the Greek of 4:26. Jesus' teaching that evil comes from the heart (Mark 7:21–23) echoes 4:23. Christian writers from the fathers to the Puritans made 4:23 a key text for the 'keeping of the heart' (John Flavel wrote a treatise by that name in 1668).

echoes: 1 Chronicles 22:5; 1 Chronicles 29:1; Deuteronomy 5:32; Joshua 1:7; Psalm 1; Matthew 7:13–14; Mark 7:21–23; Hebrews 12:12–13; Judges 5:31

settings.by: A father, quoting his own father
settings.to: His sons (plural), or a teacher's pupils
settings.when: as the teaching passes to a third generation
settings.why: To show that this teaching is not one man's opinion but an inheritance; the son should value it as the father once learned to value it.
settings.readers: Jewish readers heard Solomon recalling David's charge (1 Kings 2:1–4).
views: A father passes on what his own father taught him.
The plural 'sons' and the general 'a father' suggest a teacher and a class.

settings.to: His son
settings.when: as the son chooses his way of life
settings.why: To make the choice vivid: the road of wisdom gets brighter and safer, the path of the wicked darker. The son is to avoid even setting foot on the wrong path.

settings.to: His son
settings.when: as the son learns self-control
settings.why: To teach that wisdom must govern the whole person, from the inner heart to the mouth, eyes and feet.

title: Honey on her lips, water from your own well
sum: Chapter 5 is the father's first full warning about the strange woman. Her lips drip honey and her speech is smooth, but she leads to wormwood and a two-edged sword; her feet go down to death (5:3–6). The son must keep away from her door, or he will lose his strength, his money and his years to strangers and end his life groaning, 'How I hated discipline!' (5:7–14).

Then the father turns to marriage with images of water: drink from your own cistern, let your spring be blessed, "Take your joy from the woman you married when you were young" (5:15–18). The chapter ends with a reminder that the LORD sees every road, and that the wicked are caught in the ropes of their own sin (5:21–23).
readings: Read as sex education

The chapter is frank about desire. It does not tell the young man to suppress it but to find it in marriage: 'be lost in love for her always' (5:19). Many modern readers value its positive view of married love.
Read allegorically

Jewish and Christian readers also took the cistern and well as one's own Torah or teacher, and the strange woman as false doctrine; Origen and others read the passage as the soul's choice between Wisdom and heresy.

views.H: A young man's 'strength' and 'hard work' (5:10) are his property and future. An affair could cost him his estate through compensation to the husband or ruin. 'The assembly and the community' (5:14) is the town or clan gathered to judge.
views.C: Scholars note the poem's structure: warning (5:1–6), consequences (5:7–14), praise of marriage (5:15–20), conclusion (5:21–23). The water images of 5:15–18 are hard to follow in places, especially 5:16, which the Greek changed into a prohibition.
views.W: Egyptian instructions also warn against the strange woman and praise marriage. The Instruction of Any advises: 'Take a wife while you are young, that she may make a son for you.' Love songs from Egypt use 'my sister' and images of water and gardens, as the Song of Songs does.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition used 5:15 of drinking from one's own learning and of honoring one's teacher. The Talmud praises the man who loves his wife as himself and honors her more than himself (Bavli Yevamot 62b), in the spirit of 5:18–19. The strange woman was read as heresy (Bavli Avodah Zarah 17a).
views.X: Christian teachers have used 5:15–20 against adultery and in praise of marriage, sometimes alongside 1 Corinthians 7:2–5. The Song of Songs parallels show that the Bible treats married desire as good. The 'two-edged sword' (5:4) reappears in Hebrews 4:12 and Revelation 1:16 for the word of God.

deep.b:
In the dry hills of Judah, water was wealth. A family's cistern, cut in the rock and plastered to hold the winter rains, was private property, and a well or spring was a gift to be guarded. The father uses these images for a man's wife and the love they share. To 'drink the water your own cistern holds' (5:15) is to find delight at home; to let 'your springs spill out into the street' (5:16) is to waste what belongs to the household.

The Song of Songs uses the same picture: the bride is 'a garden locked, a spring sealed' and 'a well of living water' (Song of Songs 4:12, 15). Folly reverses it: 'Water you steal tastes sweet' (9:17). The images speak to the man, but they honor the wife: she is not property to be used but a blessing in which he should rejoice (5:18). Ecclesiastes 9:9 gives similar advice.

echoes: Song of Songs 4:11–15; Ecclesiastes 9:9; Malachi 2:14–16; Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22; Hebrews 4:12; Hebrews 13:4; 1 Corinthians 7:2–5

settings.what: Honey on her lips; drink from your own well
settings.to: His son, unmarried or newly married
settings.when: as the son reaches the age of marriage and its temptations
settings.why: To show the son where the strange woman's sweetness ends, what an affair costs a man and his household, and that desire belongs at home with the wife of his youth. Knowing the speaker is a father to a son explains the frankness: this is a parent's talk about sex.
settings.readers: For Judeans after the exile, the warnings protected families and family land; some scholars link them with the debates over marriage in Ezra and Nehemiah.
views: Most read the chapter as a warning against affairs with married women.
Some read it as a warning against marriage outside the community (Washington).

title: Pledges, the ant and fire in the lap
sum: Chapter 6 gathers four short lessons before returning to the strange woman. Do not stand good for another man's debt, and if you have, get out of it at once (6:1–5). "Go to the ant, you lazy one" (6:6), and learn to work without being told. Watch out for the troublemaker who signals with eyes, feet and fingers (6:12–15). And know the seven things the LORD hates, ending with the one who sets brothers quarreling (6:16–19).

Then the father warns again against another man's wife (6:20–35). Teaching is a lamp; it will guard you from her eyelids. A prostitute costs a loaf of bread, but adultery costs your life. Can a man carry fire against his chest and not be burned? A thief can repay, but the betrayed husband will accept no payment.
readings: Read as practical advice
The chapter's first half is the most down-to-earth part of chapters 1–9: money, work and reputation. It shows that wisdom covers everyday decisions.
Read as moral teaching
The list of seven abominations (6:16–19) and the warning against adultery have been read as summaries of the moral law, close to the Ten Commandments: false witness, murder, adultery.

views.H: Standing surety was common in a world of small loans and harvest failures; Proverbs' repeated warnings suggest many were ruined by it. The ant was a familiar sight on threshing floors at harvest. The law of theft (6:30–31) and the husband's right to revenge (6:34–35) reflect actual legal customs.
views.C: Many scholars think 6:1–19 interrupts the father's warnings about the strange woman and was inserted from a collection of short instructions, since its style resembles chapters 10–29. 6:10–11 appears again in 24:33–34. The Greek adds the bee (6:8a–c).
views.W: Lists of what a god hates appear in Egyptian texts; the 'six, and seven' pattern is found in Ugaritic poetry. The Laws of Hammurabi (129) let a betrayed husband decide whether his wife and her lover live or die, as 6:34–35 assumes the husband decides.
views.J: The Mishnah reads 6:22 as the Torah's companionship in this world, in the grave and in the world to come (Mishnah Avot 6:9). The Talmud distinguishes the 'lamp' of a commandment from the 'light' of Torah (6:23; Bavli Sotah 21a). Rabbinic teachers used the ant as a model of honest work.
views.X: Christian moralists used 6:16–19 in teaching on sin. Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus the 'guarantor' of a better covenant, which some read beside 6:1–5: Christ did what the father advises against, standing surety for others' debts. The ant became a favorite emblem of diligence in Christian art and preaching.

echoes: Genesis 43:9; Hebrews 7:22; Exodus 20:13–16; Exodus 22:1–4; Deuteronomy 6:6–9; Psalm 119:105; Leviticus 20:10; Numbers 35:31; 30:24–28; 24:30–34

settings.what: Get out of a rash pledge
settings.to: His son, a young man with property
settings.when: after he has stood good for someone else's debt
settings.why: To get him out of a dangerous promise before it ruins him. The urgency (do not sleep, 6:4) shows how real the danger was.

settings.to: The lazy one, addressed directly
settings.when: as a general lesson; the ant's summer gathering is the example
settings.why: To shame laziness with the example of a tiny creature that works without a boss, and to warn that poverty comes suddenly.

settings.what: The troublemaker and seven things the LORD hates
settings.to: The son, learning to recognize dangerous people
settings.when: as he enters public life
settings.why: To help him recognize the man who stirs up trouble by signals and lies, and to teach that the LORD hates most of all whatever destroys a community.

settings.by: A father, with the mother's teaching
settings.to: His son
settings.when: as the son is drawn to another man's wife
settings.why: To show that the parents' teaching will guard him, and to argue that adultery is not only wrong but self-destructive: the husband will take revenge, and no payment will satisfy him.
settings.readers: Later readers took 6:20–23 as words about the Torah itself, lamp and light.
views: A real father warns his son, as parents did in Israel's villages and towns (Westermann; Golka).
A teacher addresses a pupil as 'my son', as Egyptian scribal instructions do (Carr; Crenshaw).
The talk was kept and placed here by the editors of Persian-period Judea to form young men for life in the community (Fox; Washington).

title: What I saw from my window
sum: Chapter 7 tells a story. The father urges the son to keep his words and to call Wisdom 'my sister' (7:1–5). Then he describes what he saw from his window: a senseless young man walking at dusk toward a certain house, and a woman coming out to meet him, dressed like a prostitute, loud and restless (7:6–13).

She kisses him and makes her speech: she has paid her vows and has sacrificial meat at home; her bed is spread with Egyptian linen and perfumed with myrrh; her husband is away until the full moon (7:14–20). He follows her 'as an ox walks to the slaughter', like a bird into a trap, not knowing that his life is at stake (7:22–23). The father ends: her house is the road to Sheol (7:24–27).
readings: Read as a real warning
The story is vivid and specific: a real temptation, a real woman, a real young man. Many readers take it as a parent's warning drawn from life.
Read as a parable

Others note that the father 'sees' things he could not see from a window (the woman's speech, the young man's thoughts) and read the story as a constructed parable, setting up the contrast with Wisdom in chapter 8. The Greek, which makes the woman the one at the window, shows that early readers already shaped the scene.

views.H: The setting is a city street at night, with houses whose upper windows have lattices. The woman's household has means: imported linens, spices, and a husband away on business. The peace offering (7:14) meant fresh meat at home, a real feast.
views.C: Scholars debate the woman's identity (see chapter 2). Boström's theory of a foreign cult of a love goddess drew on 7:14; most now reject it. The text of 7:22 is damaged. The story uses the forms of a wisdom 'example story', like 24:30–34.
views.W: The 'woman at the window' is a motif in Phoenician ivories found at Nimrud and Samaria, often linked to a goddess or to sacred prostitution. Egyptian instructions warn of women whose husbands are away: the Instruction of Any says the woman far from her husband tells you every day 'I am pretty' when she has no witnesses.
views.J: Rabbinic readers took the woman as the evil inclination or as idolatry; the Qumran poem 4Q184, 'The Wiles of the Wicked Woman', develops the portrait into a figure of evil itself. 7:2–3 was connected with tefillin and with guarding the Torah.
views.X: The church fathers read the woman as heresy or the world's seductions, and the young man as the soul. Modern Christian teaching uses the chapter in its plain sense, on sexual temptation. The image of the ox led to slaughter (7:22) also appears for the innocent in Isaiah 53:7 and Jeremiah 11:19, a contrast many preachers note.

deep.b:
The chapter has two women and a man between them. Wisdom is to be the son's 'sister' (7:4), the word for a beloved bride in the Song of Songs. The strange woman is his seducer. The father's camera follows the young man into the dark (7:9), shows us the woman's dress and manner (7:10–12), lets us hear her speech (7:14–20) and then shows the end (7:22–23).

Feminist readers note that the woman is described entirely from the outside, through the eyes of a man looking from his window, and that her movements in public are treated as signs of danger (7:11–12). Others note that the young man is called 'senseless' (7:7) and that the story's purpose is to warn men about their own folly. The woman's speech uses religious and romantic language (vows, peace offerings, 'love until morning') to make betrayal sound like a celebration, which is why the father stresses her 'smooth lips' (7:21).

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:8; Deuteronomy 32:10; Song of Songs 4:9–14; Judges 5:28; 2 Kings 9:30; Genesis 38:14–15; Leviticus 7:15–16; Isaiah 53:7; Jeremiah 11:19

settings.to: His son
settings.when: before the story he is about to tell
settings.why: To give the son a better love to set against the strange woman: Wisdom as his sister and bride.

settings.what: The story at dusk, with the woman's speech (7:14–20)
settings.by: The father, as eyewitness and narrator; within it, the strange woman speaks
settings.to: His son, listening; inside the story, the woman speaks to a senseless young man
settings.when: one evening, as the father watches from his window
settings.why: To let the son see temptation from outside before he meets it from inside: to show how it works, step by step, and where it ends. The woman's speech is quoted so the son will recognize its sweet religious language.
settings.readers: Later readers used the story to warn against heresy and against every attractive road to ruin.
views: The father reports a real scene.
A teaching story built for the purpose, as the narrator knows more than a watcher could.

Scholars who place chapters 1–9 in a school or in Persian-period Judea read the story as a set piece kept to train young men to resist adultery and, for some, marriage outside the community (Washington).

settings.to: His sons
settings.when: at the end of the story
settings.why: To draw the lesson in one line: her house is a road to Sheol.

title: The LORD acquired me, the first of his way
sum: Chapter 8 is Wisdom's great speech. She stands at the gates and calls to every human being (8:1–5). Her words are straight and true, better than silver and gold (8:6–11). Kings reign through her, and she loves those who love her and gives them lasting wealth (8:12–21).

Then she tells of her origin: "The LORD acquired me, the first of his way, / before his works of long ago" (8:22). She was born before the deeps and the mountains, was present when he set the heavens and marked the horizon on the sea, and was beside him as a craftsman, his delight, playing before him and delighting in the human race (8:23–31). She ends: whoever finds her finds life, and whoever hates her loves death (8:32–36).
readings: Read as poetry

Many scholars read Wisdom as a bold poetic personification: the poet gives a voice to the wisdom built into creation, to show that the teaching of the wise matches the way God made the world. On this reading 8:22–31 is not a doctrine about a heavenly being but praise of wisdom's worth and authority.
Read as revelation about a person

Jewish tradition identified Wisdom with the Torah, which existed before creation and through which God made the world. Christian tradition identified her with the Son, the Word of God, through whom all things were made. Both read 8:22–31 as speaking about a real agent of creation, and both drew on the passage for their central teaching.

views.H: Wisdom calls where public life happened: the heights, the crossroads, the city gates. Her claim that kings rule through her (8:15–16) speaks to a society where kings and officials were expected to be wise judges, like Solomon.
views.C: Most scholars date the chapter to the Persian or early Hellenistic period. They debate the meaning of qanani (8:22), nissakhti (8:23) and 'amon (8:30), and whether the poem draws on Egyptian images of Maat or Greek hymns of Isis. Some think 8:13a and 8:11 are later additions. Codex Vaticanus lacks 8:29ab and 8:32b–33.
views.W: Christa Kayatz showed close parallels with Egyptian descriptions of Maat, the beloved daughter of the creator, present at creation and given to kings. Hymns to Isis in Greek praise the goddess in the first person ('I am...'), as Wisdom praises herself. Proverbs borrows the language but subordinates Wisdom to the LORD: he 'acquired' her, and she delights before him.
views.J: Genesis Rabbah 1:1 reads 'amon as 'artisan' and Wisdom as the Torah, the blueprint God consulted to create the world. The Mishnah lists the Torah among five things God 'acquired' (Avot 6:10). Sirach 24 and Baruch 3:9–4:4 had already identified Wisdom with the law of Moses.
views.X: The New Testament applies Wisdom's language to Christ (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 1:2–3; 1 Corinthians 1:24). The church fathers read 8:22–31 as the Son speaking, and in the 300s the passage became the main battleground of the Arian controversy over whether the Son was created. The Nicene Creed's 'begotten, not made' answers the Greek of 8:22.

deep.h: Qanani: what the LORD did to Wisdom
deep.b:
The first word of Wisdom's account is a verb that has been argued over for two thousand years. Qanah most often means 'acquire, get, buy' (4:5, 7). In a few verses it seems to mean 'create' or 'make' (Genesis 14:19, 22; Deuteronomy 32:6), and in Genesis 4:1 it is used of Eve's bearing Cain. Ugaritic poems use the same root for the goddess Athirat as 'creatress of the gods'. Since Wisdom says she was 'born' (8:24–25), many modern translations have 'created' or 'brought forth'; others, following Bruce Vawter and the verb's usual meaning, keep 'acquired' or 'possessed'.

The ancient translations divided. The Greek, the Syriac and the Targum have 'created'. Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, Jewish translators of the second century AD, have 'acquired', and Jerome's Latin has 'possessed' (possedit). The Plain English Translation uses 'acquired', the verb's common sense and the one used in 4:5–7, where the son is told to 'acquire' wisdom. The notes give the other readings.

For the first Christians, Wisdom spoke of Christ. Paul calls him 'the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24); John says that the Word was with God in the beginning and all things came into being through him (John 1:1–3); Colossians calls him 'the firstborn of all creation' in whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15–16). Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 61), Tertullian (Against Praxeas 6–7) and Origen (On First Principles 1.2) quoted Proverbs 8 to show that the Son was begotten before all things. Irenaeus, unusually, identified Wisdom with the Holy Spirit (Against Heresies 4.20).

But the Greek Bible said 'The Lord created me'. About AD 318 Arius, a priest of Alexandria, wrote that before the Son 'was begotten or created or determined or founded, he was not', echoing the Greek verbs of 8:22–25. If Wisdom was created, the Son was the first and greatest creature, but not God in the full sense. His opponents answered that God was never without his Wisdom, so the Son had no beginning. The Council of Nicaea in 325 declared the Son 'begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father', and condemned those who said 'there was when he was not'.

The verse itself still had to be explained. Athanasius argued at length (Orations against the Arians 2.44–82) that 'created me a beginning of his ways for his works' speaks of the human nature the Word took on for the work of salvation, while 'before all the hills he begets me' (8:25) speaks of his eternal birth from the Father. Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 30) and Augustine (On the Trinity 1.12) followed the same rule: what is lowly in Scripture's words about the Son belongs to his humanity. Jerome's 'possessed' removed the problem from the Latin Bible.

deep.h: The Jewish reading: Wisdom as Torah
deep.b:
Already in Sirach, about 180 BC, Wisdom tells how she came forth from the mouth of the Most High, sought a resting place among the nations and was told to dwell in Jacob, and the writer adds: 'All this is the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law that Moses commanded us' (Sirach 24:3–23). Baruch says of Wisdom: 'She is the book of the commandments of God, the law that endures forever' (Baruch 4:1).

The rabbis took up this identification. Genesis Rabbah opens with 8:30: the Torah says, 'I was the craftsman's tool of the Holy One.' A king who builds a palace uses an architect's plans; 'so the Holy One looked into the Torah and created the world'. The midrash reads the first word of Genesis, bereshit, 'with reshit', as 'with the Torah', because the Torah is called reshit in 8:22 (Genesis Rabbah 1:1). The Mishnah lists five things God 'acquired', the Torah first, quoting 8:22 (Avot 6:10). For Jewish readers, then, 8:22–31 teaches that the Torah is older than the world and is the pattern of its order, which is why studying it is a share in God's own wisdom.

echoes: Genesis 1:1–10; Genesis 14:19–22; Deuteronomy 32:6; Job 28:23–27; Job 38:4–11; Psalm 104:24; Sirach 24:1–23; Baruch 3:9–4:4; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–8:1; John 1:1–3; 1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 1:2–3; Revelation 3:14

settings.to: All people at the city gates: men, the naive, fools, and rulers
settings.when: in public, in daylight, in answer to the strange woman's whispered invitation of chapter 7
settings.why: To show that her words are straight, more valuable than wealth, and the source of good government, and that she loves those who love her. Coming after chapter 7, the speech offers the young man a better invitation.
settings.readers: Later readers heard the Torah calling in the houses of study, or Christ calling in the gospel.

settings.to: The same listeners; the poem is part of her appeal
settings.when: as she gives her credentials
settings.why: To prove her authority: she is older than the world, was present when the LORD made it, and delights in human beings. Her teaching is trustworthy because it matches the order of creation. In its setting the poem is an argument for listening to her (8:32), not a separate creed.
settings.readers: For Jewish readers it became the charter of the Torah's pre-existence; for Christians, a key text about the Son, fought over at Nicaea.
views: Wisdom is a poetic figure for God's own skill and the order of the world (most critical scholars).
Wisdom is the Torah, created before the world as its plan (Sirach 24; Genesis Rabbah 1:1).
Wisdom is the Word of God, begotten not made (Nicene churches).
Wisdom is the Son as God's first creation (Arius; Jehovah's Witnesses).

settings.to: 'Sons', the listeners she has addressed
settings.when: at the end of her speech
settings.why: To press for a decision: finding her is life and missing her is death. She uses the father's own words (5:7; 7:24), so her voice and his are one.

traditions.q: Is Wisdom in Proverbs 8 the eternal Son of God, a created being, or a figure of speech?
views: Wisdom's words are rightly applied to the eternal Word, 'begotten, not made', following Nicaea and the fathers; 'created' is read of his humanity. The liturgy also applies 8:22–35 to Mary by accommodation, as the 'Seat of Wisdom', in its feasts of the Virgin, and reads 8:22–31 on Trinity Sunday.

Christ is the Wisdom of God, to whom Hagia Sophia was dedicated. Following Athanasius and Gregory the Theologian, 'created' refers to the incarnation and 'he begets me' to the eternal birth; 9:1–11 is read at Vespers on feasts of the Mother of God, in whom Wisdom built her house.

Calvin and the Reformed tradition read Wisdom in Proverbs 8 as the eternal Son, while warning against building doctrine on the poem's details; many modern Reformed scholars treat it as a personification that the New Testament fulfills in Christ.

Divided: some read Proverbs 8 directly as the pre-incarnate Christ; many evangelical commentators, such as Derek Kidner and Bruce Waltke, read Wisdom as a personification of God's attribute that the New Testament applies to Christ, without taking 'acquired' or 'born' as statements about the Son's origin.

Wisdom is Jesus in his prehuman existence, created by Jehovah as 'the beginning of his way'; the New World Translation renders 8:22 'Jehovah produced me', and Colossians 1:15's 'firstborn of all creation' is read as the first one created.

title: Two feasts
sum: Chapter 9 closes the introduction with two portraits. Wisdom has built her house with seven pillars, prepared meat and mixed wine, and sent her servants to call from the heights: "Who is naive? Let him come over here!" (9:4). Her invitation is to bread, wine and life (9:5–6).

In the middle stands a set of sayings on teaching: correct a mocker and he will hate you; correct the wise and he will love you (9:7–9). The motto returns: "The start of wisdom is the fear of the LORD" (9:10). Then Woman Folly sits at her door on the same heights and calls the same naive with the same words, offering stolen water and secret bread. Her guests do not know that the shades are there, and that they are already in Sheol's depths (9:13–18).
readings: Read as the end of a gate

Chapters 1–9 began with a gang's invitation to 'come with us' (1:11) and end with two invitations to 'come over here'. The reader who has heard the father must choose which voice to follow before entering the collection of sayings that starts in chapter 10.
Read sacramentally

Christian readers from the early centuries saw in Wisdom's house the Church, in her bread and mixed wine the Eucharist, and in her servants the apostles. Jewish readers saw the house of study and the Torah's bread.

views.H: A house with seven pillars would be a grand building, a palace or a temple. Feasts with butchered meat and mixed wine were for weddings, sacrifices and royal occasions. Both women call from 'the town's high places', where public announcements were made.
views.C: The chapter has a clear three-part structure (9:1–6, 7–12, 13–18). Many think 9:7–12 is an insertion. The pairing of Wisdom and Folly sums up chapters 1–9, and many scholars think the same editor composed chapter 9 as the gateway to the collections. The Greek adds three verses after 9:12 and three after 9:18.
views.W: Building a house for a deity and celebrating with a banquet is a familiar ancient pattern: Baal's palace in the Ugaritic poems is completed with a feast. Some scholars see Wisdom's house as a temple; most see a symbolic house for her teaching.
views.J: The Talmud reads Wisdom's house as the world God made, and the seven pillars as the seven days of creation (Bavli Sanhedrin 38a). Wisdom's bread and wine are the Torah: 'Come, eat my bread' became an invitation to study.
views.X: Cyprian (Letter 63) and Augustine (City of God 17.20) read Wisdom's feast as the Eucharist and her house as the Church, or as the human body of Christ. Orthodox churches read 9:1–11 at Vespers on feasts of the Mother of God, seeing the house Wisdom built as the Virgin in whom the Word took flesh. Jesus' parable of the wedding banquet (Matthew 22:1–10) uses the same pattern of servants sent with an invitation.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three invitations
deep.b: My own reading: chapters 1–9 are framed by three invitations. The first is the gang's: 'Come with us!' (1:11), a call to share loot, with 'one money bag for all of us' (1:14). The last two are Wisdom's and Folly's, in the same words: 'Who is naive? Let him come over here!' (9:4, 16). The gang offers a shared purse, Folly offers stolen water and hidden bread, and Wisdom offers bread and wine she prepared herself. Two of the three offers are about taking what belongs to others, and both end in death (1:18–19; 9:18). Wisdom's alone is a gift. Commentators often note the parallel of 9:4 and 9:16; reading the gang's invitation as the first of three is my suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 2:2–3; Isaiah 25:6; Isaiah 55:1–3; Sirach 24:19–21; Matthew 22:1–10; Luke 14:16–24; John 6:35; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26; Psalm 111:10; Job 28:28

settings.by: Wisdom, through her serving girls and in her own voice
settings.to: The naive and the senseless of the town
settings.when: after she has built her house and prepared the meal
settings.why: To invite those who most need her to leave their naivety and live. The feast shows that wisdom is generous and joyful, not grim.
settings.readers: Jewish readers heard the invitation to Torah study; Christian readers, the invitation of the gospel and the Lord's table.

settings.to: Those who teach and those who are taught
settings.when: between the two invitations
settings.why: To explain why some accept Wisdom's invitation and others do not: the mocker resents correction, the wise welcome it, and each bears the result of his choice.

settings.by: Woman Folly; the narrator adds the last line
settings.to: The same naive passers-by
settings.when: from her doorway on the same heights
settings.why: To warn that folly sounds like wisdom and uses the same words, and to show where her feast really is: among the dead.
settings.readers: Later readers saw in Folly every false teaching that imitates the true.
